top_level_objectives: Decompose a 2D vector into horizontal and vertical components using right-triangle trigonometry.
Demonstrate vector addition graphically using the tip-to-tail method.
Explain the physical significance of initial velocity components (v0x and v0y) in projectile motion.
Analyze how horizontal and vertical motions are independent in a gravity field.
Predict and manipulate how changing launch speed and angle influences a projectile's range, maximum height, and flight duration.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vectors as quantities with both magnitude and direction, and demonstrate how to resolve them into x and y components using right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: A large, interactive 3D vector arrow floating in the center of the room.
A coordinate grid projected on the floor or table showing x and y axes.
Dashed projection lines extending from the vector tip to the axes, forming a right triangle.
Floating mathematical formulas showing Ax = A cos(theta) and Ay = A sin(theta) that update dynamically.
student_actions: Grab and rotate the vector arrow to change its angle relative to the horizontal axis.
Stretch the vector to change its magnitude.
Observe how the components on the x and y axes scale dynamically and watch the trigonometry calculations update in real time.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate the concept of vector addition using the tip-to-tail method and show how the resultant vector relates to the individual component sums.
key_visuals: Two distinct vectors of different colors (Vector A in blue, Vector B in green) resting on a coordinate grid.
A dotted red vector representing the resultant vector R.
Floating mathematical expressions showing Rx = Ax + Bx and Ry = Ay + By.
student_actions: Physically drag Vector B and align its tail with the tip of Vector A.
Observe the resultant Vector R snap into place from the tail of A to the tip of B.
Toggle component grids to visually confirm that the horizontal and vertical lengths of R are the exact sums of A and B's respective components.

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply vector decomposition to a physical projectile launcher, demonstrating how launch speed and angle dictate the initial horizontal and vertical velocity components.
key_visuals: A stylized 3D cannon/launcher resting on a flat surface.
An initial velocity vector arrow (v0) emerging from the barrel, splitting into a horizontal component arrow (v0x) and a vertical component arrow (v0y).
Interactive sliders for Launch Angle and Launch Speed.
student_actions: Adjust the Launch Angle slider and observe how a steeper angle increases the vertical velocity component while decreasing the horizontal component.
Adjust the Launch Speed slider to scale the overall magnitude of the initial velocity vector and its components.
Predict how these component changes will affect the upcoming launch.

scenes.brief_purpose: Illustrate the fundamental independence of horizontal and vertical motions by comparing a dropped projectile to a horizontally launched projectile.
key_visuals: Two launcher apparatuses side-by-side: one configured to drop a ball straight down, and one configured to launch a ball horizontally.
Horizontal grid lines tracking vertical position.
Real-time velocity vector arrows attached to both spheres.
student_actions: Press a launch button to release both spheres simultaneously.
Use a time-scrubbing slider to slow down, pause, or reverse the motion.
Observe that both spheres fall at the exact same vertical rate and hit the ground at the same moment, proving that horizontal motion does not affect vertical gravitational acceleration.

scenes.brief_purpose: Analyze the entire parabolic trajectory of a projectile, tracking how the velocity components change or remain constant throughout flight.
key_visuals: A fully traced parabolic trajectory path left by a launched projectile.
A slow-motion projectile traveling along this path with active velocity vector arrows (vx, vy, and total velocity v) attached to it.
Visual indicators showing when the vertical velocity reaches zero at the peak (apex).
student_actions: Launch a projectile and watch it trace a parabola.
Scrub through the flight timeline to inspect the velocity vectors at different points (ascent, apex, descent).

Observe that the horizontal velocity vector (vx) remains completely constant throughout flight, while the vertical velocity vector (vy) decreases to zero at the apex and grows in the downward direction during descent.

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply understanding of launch components, angles, and speed to solve practical target challenges, demonstrating how these variables affect range and maximum height.
key_visuals: A virtual target hoop placed at a distance in the student's physical room.
An obstacle (such as a wall) placed between the launcher and the target, requiring a specific high-arc or low-arc trajectory.
A live scorecard and trajectory prediction arc that can be toggled on or off.
student_actions: Analyze the target's distance and height, and estimate the necessary horizontal and vertical velocity components.
Manipulate the launch angle and speed sliders to clear the obstacle and land the projectile inside the target hoop.
Iterate on different launch profiles (e.g., high-angle vs. low-angle) to understand how different combinations of vx and vy can reach the same horizontal range.
